lessons.title: Relative clauses that control meaning
lessons.description: Distinguish identifying information from an added comment.

content.heading: Identify or add a comment
content.text: A defining relative clause identifies which person or thing you mean. A non-defining clause adds information about an already identified referent and is set off by commas. The punctuation changes the claim: it can distinguish a selected group from a comment about the whole group.
examples: Employees who work remotely need secure access.
The employees, who work remotely, need secure access.

content.heading: Choose the reference carefully
content.text: Use whose for possession, including possession by organizations. In formal writing, a preposition may come before which or whom. Do not use that after a comma in a non-defining relative clause. Which can also refer to a whole preceding proposition, so check what your reader will understand.
examples: The charity, whose offices flooded, needs temporary space.
The deadline moved, which surprised the team.

content.heading: Apply and test the interpretation
content.text: Write two versions of a notice about researchers receiving a grant. In one version, identify only the researchers studying rivers; in the other, explain that all the researchers study rivers. Read each aloud with its pauses, then ask whether a reader could infer the existence of a second group.
examples: Researchers who study rivers received funding.
The researchers, who study rivers, received funding.

questions.prompt: Which sentence identifies only the managers with budget responsibility?
options: Managers who control budgets must attend.
Managers, who control budgets, must attend.
All managers must attend, regardless of responsibility.
Managers must attend, which controls budgets.
questions.explanation: Without commas, who control budgets restricts the group to the managers with that responsibility.

questions.prompt: Complete: The foundation, ___ director resigned, appointed an interim leader.
options: which
whose
that
whom
questions.explanation: Whose expresses the relationship between the foundation and its director.

questions.prompt: In “The deadline moved, which surprised the team,” what does which refer to?
options: Only the noun team
An unnamed person
The fact that the deadline moved
A particular kind of deadline
questions.explanation: Here which comments on the whole preceding event, rather than identifying a noun.

lessons.title: Report claims without endorsing them
lessons.description: Control attribution, reporting verbs, and cautious passive structures.

content.heading: Separate a claim from your commitment
content.text: Reporting language tells a reader who holds a view and how strongly you endorse it. Say the author argues when presenting a reasoned position, suggests for a tentative interpretation, and demonstrates only when the supporting evidence justifies that strength. Reporting a statement does not automatically establish its truth.
examples: The researcher suggests that access affects participation.
The editorial argues for longer opening hours.

content.heading: Place the reporting time correctly
content.text: Formal reporting passives include it is believed that and the subject is believed to. Use a perfect infinitive when the reported event precedes the reporting situation. Keep the original level of uncertainty: a report that someone may have left should not become a confident statement that they left.
examples: The building is believed to have opened in 1910.
It is reported that the team may withdraw.

content.heading: Revise an overconfident summary
content.text: Take the claim “The campaign caused sales to rise” and imagine that your only source is an interview with the campaign manager. Attribute the interpretation, distinguish it from independently verified figures, and retain uncertainty. Compare the result with your original sentence and underline the words that protect the source boundary.
examples: The manager attributes the rise in sales to the campaign.
Sales rose, but the interview alone cannot establish the cause.

questions.prompt: Which reporting verb is most cautious for a possible interpretation?
options: Proves conclusively
Guarantees
Settles beyond doubt
Suggests
questions.explanation: Suggests presents an interpretation as tentative rather than as established proof.

questions.prompt: Choose the form showing that the opening happened before the current belief.
options: The library is believed to have opened in 1910.
The library is believed opening in 1910.
The library believes to open in 1910.
The library is believed to opening in 1910.
questions.explanation: To have opened is a perfect infinitive placing the opening before the present reporting situation.

questions.prompt: A manager says advertising caused a rise. Which summary accurately attributes the claim?
options: Advertising certainly caused the rise.
The manager attributes the rise to advertising.
The figures prove advertising was the only cause.
Everyone agrees advertising caused the rise.
questions.explanation: The answer identifies the source of the causal interpretation without endorsing it as independently established.

lessons.title: Use participle clauses safely
lessons.description: Compress ideas while keeping subjects and time relationships clear.

content.heading: Keep the understood subject stable
content.text: An introductory participle clause usually shares its understood subject with the main clause. In “Walking home, I noticed the sign,” I was walking. If the main subject is a sign, the sentence may accidentally imply that the sign was walking. Rewrite the clause when the subject connection becomes unclear.
examples: Walking home, I noticed the sign.
As I walked home, the sign caught my attention.

content.heading: Express sequence and voice
content.text: An ing clause often presents an accompanying action or reason. Having plus a past participle can make an earlier action explicit. A past participle can express a passive meaning. Compression is useful only when the logical relationship remains clear; a full clause may be better for a complex contrast or condition.
examples: Having checked the figures, Jo submitted the report.
Written for beginners, the guide avoids specialist terms.

content.heading: Run a subject check
content.text: Revise “Having reviewed the contract, several errors became clear.” Ask who reviewed it, then make that person the subject or restore a full clause. Finally write a sentence about your own learning using having plus a past participle. Name the earlier action and the later result before you compress them.
examples: Having reviewed the contract, we identified several errors.
After we reviewed the contract, several errors became clear.

questions.prompt: Which introductory clause has a clear matching subject?
options: Having checked the map, the route looked shorter.
Walking to class, the rain started.
Having checked the map, Leena chose the shorter route.
Written by an expert, I enjoyed the guide.
questions.explanation: Leena is both the person who checked the map and the person who chose the route.

questions.prompt: What does having checked emphasize in “Having checked the figures, Jo submitted the report”?
options: The check will happen tomorrow.
The report checked Jo.
Submission and checking are always identical actions.
The check occurred before submission.
questions.explanation: Having plus past participle explicitly marks an action completed before the main event.

questions.prompt: Which revision fixes “Having reviewed the contract, several errors became clear”?
options: Having reviewed the contract, we identified several errors.
Having reviewed the contract, several errors were reviewing.
Having reviewed the contract, the errors reviewed us.
Having reviewing the contract, errors were clear.
questions.explanation: Making we the main subject gives the participle clause a logical human reviewer.

lessons.title: Academic verbs and their partners
lessons.description: Use argument verbs with the complements they naturally take.

content.heading: Learn the grammatical partner
content.text: An advanced word is useful only when you can fit it into a sentence. Distinguish attribute something to a cause from result in an outcome and result from a cause. Treat the preposition as part of the expression. Reversing it can reverse the relationship you intend to describe.
examples: The team attributed the delay to a missing permit.
The missing permit resulted in a delay.

content.heading: Distinguish argument functions
content.text: Challenge questions a claim; corroborate supplies supporting evidence; reconcile explains how apparently conflicting observations can fit together. These verbs describe different intellectual actions. Do not replace them mechanically with show. Choose a verb by asking what the evidence actually does in relation to an existing argument.
examples: The second survey corroborates the earlier finding.
The new model reconciles the two estimates.

content.heading: Build a precise mini-summary
content.text: Write three sentences about an imagined study: one explaining an outcome, one describing supporting evidence, and one acknowledging a conflicting result. Circle each verb and its following preposition or clause. Replace a verb if it exaggerates the certainty of the evidence, then read the summary as a connected argument.
examples: The authors attribute lower attendance to transport costs.
A later interview study supports, but does not prove, that explanation.

questions.prompt: Complete: The delay resulted ___ a missing permit.
options: at
from
for
by
questions.explanation: Result from introduces the cause; result in introduces the consequence.

questions.prompt: A new independent dataset supports an earlier finding. Which verb fits?
options: Contradicts
Evades
Corroborates
Withholds
questions.explanation: Corroborate means supply additional support for an existing statement or finding.

questions.prompt: What does it mean to reconcile two apparently conflicting observations?
options: Delete one without explanation
Prove both observations false automatically
Repeat them in capital letters
Explain how they can be compatible
questions.explanation: Reconciling observations accounts for their apparent conflict rather than merely ignoring one.

lessons.title: Idioms, literal meaning, and audience
lessons.description: Recognize common figurative language and choose when to paraphrase.

content.heading: Understand the figurative image
content.text: An idiom has a conventional meaning that may not follow directly from its individual words. A stumbling block is an obstacle; on the fence means undecided; a long shot is an attempt with a low chance of success. Learn each expression through a situation and a complete example, rather than translating each word.
examples: Funding remains the main stumbling block.
I am on the fence about moving.

content.heading: Match the audience and purpose
content.text: An idiom can make an informal conversation vivid, but unfamiliar imagery may obscure instructions for an international audience. Understand it when you hear it, and choose a plain equivalent when clarity matters. Register is contextual: neither a figurative expression nor its formal alternative is automatically superior.
examples: Informal: Let us touch base on Tuesday.
Clear scheduling: Let us discuss progress on Tuesday.

content.heading: Practise a two-version message
content.text: Write a friendly update using two familiar idioms, then rewrite it for a new colleague who is learning English. Preserve the action, uncertainty, and timing. Check that your plain version does not accidentally turn a low probability into an impossibility, or an undecided opinion into a rejection.
examples: It is a long shot, but we will apply.
Success is unlikely, but we will apply.

questions.prompt: “I am on the fence about the offer” most likely means what?
options: I have not decided whether to accept.
I have already rejected it.
I am repairing outdoor furniture.
I have accepted without hesitation.
questions.explanation: On the fence conventionally describes an undecided position.

questions.prompt: Which paraphrase preserves “It is a long shot”?
options: It is certain to fail.
It has a low chance of succeeding.
It is guaranteed to succeed.
It requires a camera.
questions.explanation: A long shot is unlikely to succeed, but success remains possible.

questions.prompt: Which instruction is clearest for an audience unfamiliar with workplace idioms?
options: Please touch base and circle back at some point.
Keep your ear to the ground and run with it.
Please discuss progress with me on Tuesday.
Move the needle when the ball is in your court.
questions.explanation: The plain instruction names both the action and time without requiring knowledge of several idioms.

lessons.title: Word families and precise collocations
lessons.description: Choose the right form without relying on suffixes alone.

content.heading: Connect meaning and sentence role
content.text: A word family links related forms such as analysis, analyse, analytical, and analytically. The form depends on the sentence role: a noun can name a process, a verb describes the action, and an adjective modifies a noun. Learn a short phrase with each form instead of assuming every ending is interchangeable.
examples: We analyse the responses.
The analysis reveals a pattern.
She takes an analytical approach.

content.heading: Notice natural combinations
content.text: Collocations are conventional word combinations. We draw a distinction, reach a consensus, and pose a question. Alternatives may be understandable but less natural. Record the complete combination, including articles or prepositions where useful. Watch meaning too: reach a consensus describes agreement, whereas establish a fact concerns supporting its truth.
examples: Draw a distinction between access and use.
The panel reached a consensus on the criteria.

content.heading: Revise through a substitution test
content.text: Write a paragraph about a community survey using one word family and two collocations. Replace a noun with a verb only after rebuilding the sentence around it. Check a trusted dictionary when unsure of a form. Finish by explaining why a natural combination fits the intended action rather than merely sounding impressive.
examples: Our evaluation identified a problem.
We evaluated the service and identified a problem.

questions.prompt: Complete: The team took an ___ approach to the data.
options: analysis
analyse
analytically
analytical
questions.explanation: Approach is a noun modified by the adjective analytical.

questions.prompt: Which is a natural collocation for making a conceptual difference clear?
options: Draw a distinction
Do a distinction
Spend a distinction
Arrive a distinction
questions.explanation: Draw a distinction is the conventional combination for identifying a meaningful difference.

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly changes the noun evaluation into a verb construction?
options: We evaluation the service carefully.
We evaluated the service carefully.
We were evaluate of the service.
We did evaluative the service.
questions.explanation: Evaluated is the past-tense verb, with the service as its direct object.

lessons.title: Read a pilot scheme with caution
lessons.description: Distinguish a result, an explanation, and a missing comparison.

content.heading: Original passage: an evening library trial
content.text: For six weeks, Northbank Library stayed open until nine on Wednesdays. Evening visits rose from an average of forty to seventy per week. A council newsletter described the trial as proof that extended hours brought new readers into the library. Yet the registration count changed little, and staff reported that some regular visitors had shifted their visits from afternoons to evenings. The trial also coincided with examinations at a nearby college. Students welcomed the quieter study space, while parents requested later openings on Fridays instead. The librarian recommended continuing Wednesday evenings for another term, alongside a survey asking visitors when they would otherwise have come. She also proposed comparing attendance with a similar branch that retained its usual hours. The aim, she explained, was to learn whether the change expanded access or mainly redistributed existing use.
examples: Reported evening average: forty before, seventy during.
Alternative explanations: shifted visits and examination demand.

content.heading: Separate outcome from interpretation
content.text: The passage reports a rise in evening visits, but the newsletter adds an interpretation about new readers. Registration figures and staff observations complicate that interpretation. Identify the precise outcome measured and ask whether it establishes the claimed benefit. A plausible explanation is not necessarily the only explanation supported by the situation.
examples: More evening visits does not by itself establish more unique readers.
The registration count changed little despite increased evening visits.

content.heading: Produce a qualified summary
content.text: Summarize the result in one sentence and the uncertainty in a second. Then explain why a comparison branch could help, while acknowledging that branches may differ. For unofficial IELTS-style practice, justify each answer with a phrase from the passage before checking the explanation.
examples: Evening attendance increased; its effect on total access remains unclear.
A survey can ask whether an evening visit replaced an afternoon one.

questions.prompt: What did the reported figures directly show?
options: A comparable increase in unique library members
An increase in total weekly visits across all opening hours
An increase in Wednesday evening visits
A rise of thirty new registrations per week
questions.explanation: The stated change is from forty to seventy evening visits, not a verified increase in unique readers.

questions.prompt: Why does the nearby college matter to the argument?
options: Its examinations prove that every additional visitor was a student.
Its calendar explains why existing readers registered again.
Its examination schedule makes a comparison branch unnecessary.
Its examinations offer another explanation for study-space demand.
questions.explanation: The timing of examinations could influence attendance independently of the new opening hours.

questions.prompt: What does the librarian recommend?
options: Continue the trial while gathering information about displaced visits and a comparison branch.
Continue the trial and use evening attendance alone as the success measure.
Replace Wednesday evenings with Friday openings because parents requested them.
Complete the branch comparison before allowing any further evening visits.
questions.explanation: The recommendation combines continued Wednesday access with a visitor survey and branch comparison.

lessons.title: Synthesize two views fairly
lessons.description: Find agreement beneath different emphases.

content.heading: Original passages: local food policy
content.text: Source A: A council should support local food markets because direct contact can help small growers explain their methods and build customer trust. Local origin alone, however, does not establish a low environmental impact. Production methods and transport efficiency matter too. Buyers need clear information rather than a reassuring label. Source B: Public purchasing can strengthen regional farms, provided contracts remain accessible to smaller suppliers. Requiring every ingredient to come from nearby would create difficulties when seasonal supplies are limited. A flexible policy could prioritize regional produce when suitable alternatives exist, while publishing its selection criteria. Neither source claims that geography is irrelevant. Both argue that a useful policy needs more detail than a simple local-versus-imported divide, although A emphasizes consumers and B emphasizes institutional purchasing.
examples: A prioritizes buyer information.
B prioritizes accessible contracts and flexible procurement.

content.heading: Separate shared ground from emphasis
content.text: A synthesis organizes sources around an issue rather than retelling each text in isolation. Identify where they agree, where they differ, and whether an apparent conflict concerns a different audience or situation. Preserve conditions such as provided and when suitable alternatives exist, because they define the scope of support.
examples: Both sources resist treating local origin as a sufficient rule.
A discusses consumer trust, whereas B examines procurement access.

content.heading: Draft a synthesis statement
content.text: Write a short combined summary naming one shared principle and one difference of emphasis. Attribute distinct recommendations to their sources. Avoid creating a consensus that neither author states, and do not convert a conditional preference into a universal prohibition.
examples: Both favour informed, flexible decisions; A focuses on consumers, whereas B examines public contracts.
Neither text treats every imported product as unacceptable.

questions.prompt: Which principle do both sources support?
options: Local origin provides sufficient evidence of environmental benefit.
Local-food decisions require more than a simple geographic label.
Public purchasing should use an inflexible geographic rule.
Direct consumer contact resolves the difficulties of institutional contracts.
questions.explanation: A discusses production and information; B discusses flexibility and contract access. Both reject an absolute geographic rule.

questions.prompt: Which recommendation belongs specifically to Source B?
options: Let consumers assess growers through direct conversations.
Treat production method as irrelevant if the origin is nearby.
Keep public contracts accessible to smaller suppliers.
Require regional ingredients even when seasonal alternatives are unavailable.
questions.explanation: Source B explicitly discusses the design of public purchasing contracts.

questions.prompt: Which summary overstates the sources?
options: Both favour qualified approaches to local-food decisions.
A treats information for buyers as important.
B argues for flexibility when regional supply is unsuitable.
Both insist that every ingredient must be local.
questions.explanation: B expressly warns that requiring every ingredient to be nearby would create difficulties, and A makes no universal requirement.

lessons.title: Identify a writer’s reservations
lessons.description: Read concession, evaluative wording, and a measured conclusion.

content.heading: Original passage: the frictionless museum
content.text: The museum’s new app promises a frictionless visit. Visitors can reserve a route, receive descriptions beside each object, and avoid the information desk entirely. These features will undoubtedly help some people, particularly those planning a short visit. Whether a museum should remove every moment of uncertainty is another question. An unexpected conversation with a guide or a wrong turn into an unfamiliar room can become the most memorable part of a visit. There is also the matter of visitors who prefer a printed map or cannot comfortably use a phone. The app deserves a place among the museum’s tools, but presenting it as the natural replacement for human assistance seems premature. A successful design might offer confident navigation without assuming that all wandering is wasted time. Convenience is valuable; it need not become the only measure of a cultural experience.
examples: Concession: the app will help some visitors.
Reservation: convenience is not the only value.

content.heading: Follow the rhetorical turn
content.text: A concession grants a reasonable benefit before introducing a reservation. Words such as undoubtedly do not establish that the writer supports every feature. Locate the turning question and the final recommendation. Notice how seems premature expresses caution about replacement without requiring rejection of the technology itself.
examples: The writer accepts an app as one useful tool.
The writer questions replacement, rather than the existence of the app.

content.heading: Support an interpretation
content.text: Describe the writer’s attitude using two elements: a recognized advantage and a proposed limit. Quote only a brief phrase when practising, then explain its role in your own words. Test your interpretation against the conclusion rather than selecting a single approving or critical adjective from the opening.
examples: The app should complement assistance and preserve choice.
Printed maps remain useful for visitors who do not use a phone.

questions.prompt: Which best describes the writer’s position?
options: The app is useful but should preserve alternatives and human assistance.
The app is a reasonable replacement once its route descriptions are improved.
The app is convenient mainly because human assistance has become unnecessary.
The app should remain secondary because unplanned visits are always more valuable.
questions.explanation: The writer grants convenience while questioning replacement and the assumption that all wandering is wasteful.

questions.prompt: Why does the writer mention a wrong turn?
options: To establish that the museum’s routes are too poorly marked to use
To illustrate how an unplanned experience can have value.
To suggest that guides should lead visitors away from their chosen objects
To argue that navigation should be removed from the app
questions.explanation: The example supports the argument that uncertainty is not always a defect in a museum visit.

questions.prompt: What does “seems premature” signal?
options: A prediction that the app will eventually fail altogether
An endorsement of replacement once visitors stop requesting printed maps
A cautious objection to replacing human assistance now
An admission that digital assistance has already become the only practical option
questions.explanation: Premature suggests the conclusion or action is being adopted before it is justified.

lessons.title: Listen for methods and limits
lessons.description: Track the measured outcome and the design cautions in a lecture.

content.heading: Prepare a four-part note frame
content.text: Before playing this original lecture extract, make headings for procedure, observed difference, unchanged outcome, and limitations. Predict useful grammatical signals rather than an answer: before often marks a stage, whereas however introduces a qualification. Listen once without trying to write every sentence, then fill gaps on a second play.
examples: Procedure → questions or rereading; same reading and preparation time.
Outcome notes: specific examples increased; speaker numbers did not.

content.heading: Distinguish detail from participation
content.text: The speaker compares how specifically students contributed with how many students spoke. Those are separate outcomes, so improved discussion detail does not establish that more students participated. Keep this distinction when summarizing, and note whether the speaker treats the result as tentative or conclusive.
examples: More examples ≠ more speakers.
No random assignment limits causal interpretation.

content.heading: Apply a claim audit
content.text: After listening, write one sentence beginning the activity may, followed by a specific observed benefit. Add one design limitation and the proposed improvement. Replay only the segment that supports each note. Check the transcript last so that reading does not replace listening during your first attempt.
examples: The plan adds alternating activities and an independent observer.
The benefit concerns discussion detail, not an increase in participants.

questions.prompt: What difference was observed?
options: The question group had more students contributing to discussion.
The question group recalled more simple facts from its reading.
The rereading group used more specific examples a week later.
The question group used more specific examples.
questions.explanation: The speaker reports greater specificity; materials and preparation time were matched.

questions.prompt: Which outcome did not differ?
options: The number of students who spoke
The detail in students’ discussion contributions
The usefulness of the preparation reported by teachers
The number of specific examples used a week later
questions.explanation: The speaker explicitly states no difference in the number of speakers.

questions.prompt: Why is an independent observer proposed?
options: Students had been randomly assigned but refused to follow instructions.
The instructor knew which exercise each group completed.
The previous observer had assessed discussion without knowing the exercises.
The rereading exercise took longer than the question exercise.
questions.explanation: Independent assessment would address a concern related to the instructor’s knowledge of group conditions.

lessons.listeningText: Before we move to the results, let me explain what we actually changed. Students in two seminar groups received the same reading material. One group answered brief questions before the discussion; the other simply reread the text for the same amount of time. In the following discussion, the question group referred to more specific examples. That difference was still present a week later, when students discussed a related topic without preparation. We did not find a difference in the number of students who spoke, however, so the exercise seems to have affected the detail of contributions rather than participation itself. There are two cautions. The groups already existed, and we could not randomly assign students. Also, the instructor knew which exercise each group completed. Next term, we plan to alternate the exercises across several groups and ask an independent observer to assess the discussions. For now, I would describe the activity as a useful possibility, not an established solution.

lessons.title: Listen for the actual disagreement
lessons.description: Separate shared goals from competing sequences of action.

content.heading: Listen for common ground
content.text: The speaker begins by naming areas of agreement before identifying a narrower disagreement. Draw two columns, shared goals and contested decision. This helps you resist the assumption that opposing groups disagree about everything. Listen for nobody, also, and concerns, which help mark the boundaries of the dispute.
examples: Common goal: reuse the warehouses and retain public river access.
Contested decision: appointing a builder before the study is complete.

content.heading: Follow the conditional consequence
content.text: A conditional risk is not a prediction that the worst outcome will certainly occur. Here, one possible finding could force changes to a design. Record the condition and consequence separately, then identify which action the speaker wants to delay and which activities can continue.
examples: If road capacity is inadequate → substantial design changes may be needed.
If capacity is adequate, this particular constraint may not require redesign.

content.heading: Reconstruct the proposed sequence
content.text: After two listens, explain the proposal as a sequence of three practical steps. Include one activity that can proceed immediately and the commitment that should wait. Check your summary for an accidental claim that the whole project should stop; the recording explicitly distinguishes preparation from a major commitment.
examples: Continue preliminary work; complete the study; then commit to a layout.
The speaker permits maintenance while opposing an early budget commitment.

questions.prompt: What do both groups support?
options: Selecting a builder before transport evidence is available
Using the existing warehouse layout without revision
Reusing the warehouses and retaining public river access
Prioritizing the construction schedule over public access
questions.explanation: The opening identifies these as agreed goals.

questions.prompt: What is the central disagreement?
options: Whether a preliminary design should be prepared at all
Whether public river access should be included in the design
Whether every maintenance task should wait for a builder
Whether to select a builder before the transport study is complete
questions.explanation: The speaker explicitly says the disagreement concerns the sequence of decisions.

questions.prompt: Which activity does the speaker say can continue immediately?
options: Surveys and community meetings
Committing most of the budget to the preferred layout
Appointing a builder before the transport study ends
Implementing a final road design before capacity is known
questions.explanation: The speaker lists surveys, community meetings, and maintenance as work that need not wait.

lessons.listeningText: You have heard both teams describe the riverside proposal, so I want to clarify where we agree. Nobody is suggesting that the old warehouses should remain empty indefinitely. We also agree that the public should retain access to the river. The disagreement concerns the sequence of decisions. The development group would like to select a builder before the transport study is complete, arguing that an early appointment would protect the schedule. Our group thinks that would narrow the options too soon. If the study shows that the existing road cannot handle additional traffic, the design may need substantial changes. We therefore propose completing the study first, while allowing potential builders to comment on several preliminary designs. That is not a request to postpone all work. Surveys, community meetings, and basic maintenance can continue immediately. What we want to avoid is committing most of the budget to one layout before we understand a constraint that could reshape it.

lessons.title: Listen when a researcher changes focus
lessons.description: Recognize a revised interpretation without inventing a contradiction.

content.heading: Map the original and revised question
content.text: In an extended explanation, speakers may retain earlier measurements while changing how they interpret them. Listen for the original questionnaire, the unexpected issue, and the revised scope. Write a simple before-and-after note, preserving the distinction between disliking a place and facing difficulty reaching it.
examples: Original measures: visit frequency and satisfaction.
Revised scope: ask how people reach the park.

content.heading: Notice what is retained
content.text: A revised interpretation does not necessarily mean that previous data were useless. The speaker explicitly retains satisfaction questions, but rejects treating them as a complete explanation. Listen for still and simply: small words can show continuity as well as change in academic arguments.
examples: New focus: the journey as well as facilities inside the park.
Satisfaction remains useful, but it cannot explain every attendance pattern.

content.heading: Practise a faithful paraphrase
content.text: Summarize the change using both and rather than replacing one measure with another. Then imagine a follow-up question that would distinguish low interest from poor access. Replay the conclusion and check whether your summary preserves the relationship between numerical findings and personal accounts.
examples: The report will combine figures with residents’ journey descriptions.
How easy is it for you to cross the road near the entrance?

questions.prompt: What did the original questionnaire ask about?
options: Residents’ road-crossing behaviour and entrance preferences
Visit frequency and satisfaction
How satisfied residents were with the route to the park
The relationship between activity costs and park attendance
questions.explanation: The opening identifies how often residents visited and how satisfied they were.

questions.prompt: Why might more activities inside the park be insufficient?
options: The interviews established that residents preferred fewer facilities.
Residents reported satisfaction only after new activities were offered.
Some barriers concern the journey to the park.
Low attendance was caused entirely by a lack of internal facilities.
questions.explanation: Road crossing and hard-to-find entrances are access issues that new internal activities may leave unresolved.

questions.prompt: How will the next report present evidence?
options: By replacing satisfaction data with journey descriptions
By reporting satisfaction figures without the access concerns
By treating interview accounts as an alternative to all numerical data
By combining figures with short accounts of residents’ journeys
questions.explanation: The conclusion explicitly brings numbers and experiences together.

lessons.listeningText: When we began interviewing residents about the new park, our questionnaire asked how often they visited and how satisfied they were. Those questions produced tidy numbers, but the interviews soon revealed a missing issue. Several residents enjoyed the park yet felt uneasy crossing the busy road beside it. Others said they rarely visited because the entrances were difficult to find, not because they disliked the facilities. We therefore added questions about the journey to the park. This changed our interpretation of low attendance. It would have been easy to recommend more activities inside the park, but that would not necessarily address problems outside its boundaries. We are keeping the satisfaction questions because they still tell us something useful. We are simply no longer treating them as a complete explanation of use. Our next report will present the figures together with short accounts of residents’ journeys, so that the numbers and experiences can inform each other rather than compete for attention.

lessons.title: Build a synthesis paragraph
lessons.description: Combine sources around a claim and mark the limits of agreement.

content.heading: Organize by the shared issue
content.text: A synthesis paragraph uses several sources to develop one point. Start with the issue you want to explain, then select relevant evidence from each source. Avoid a sequence of disconnected summaries. Attribute ideas clearly, especially when sources disagree or examine different groups, time periods, or outcomes.
examples: A finds better access among commuters; B identifies costs for shift workers.
A combined paragraph can compare how access differs across work schedules.

content.heading: Show the relationship between sources
content.text: Use similarly for a genuine parallel, whereas for a contrast, and extends when one source develops another. The connector must describe the evidence rather than manufacture agreement. If two studies measure different outcomes, explain that difference before combining them into a general conclusion.
examples: Both address access, but they examine different schedules.
The findings suggest benefits may depend on working patterns.

content.heading: Draft and revise a compact argument
content.text: Practise with two invented notes: Survey A reports shorter journeys for daytime commuters; Interview B records fewer services after ten at night. Write a paragraph that acknowledges both outcomes and gives a bounded conclusion. Then underline attribution, circle the connector, and remove any claim about all travellers.
examples: The timetable appears helpful for daytime commuters, while late workers may still face poor access.
The evidence concerns the surveyed groups, rather than every possible traveller.

questions.prompt: Which opening best supports synthesis?
options: The revised timetable affects daytime and late-night travellers differently.
Source A exists. Source B exists.
Every source proves the timetable is perfect.
Transport has always been interesting.
questions.explanation: The opening creates an issue around which evidence from both sources can be organized.

questions.prompt: Which connector accurately relates shorter daytime journeys and fewer late-night services?
options: Identically
Whereas
For the same reason in every case
As an exact equivalent
questions.explanation: Whereas marks a relevant contrast between outcomes for different travellers.

questions.prompt: What should the paragraph avoid claiming from these notes?
options: Daytime commuters reported shorter journeys.
Late-night services remain a concern.
Every traveller benefits equally.
The effect may depend on working patterns.
questions.explanation: The evidence explicitly differs by schedule, so equal universal benefit is unsupported.

lessons.title: Write constructive, specific feedback
lessons.description: Turn evaluation into evidence, impact, and a useful next step.

content.heading: Describe what a reader can locate
content.text: Useful feedback identifies a feature of the work rather than assigning a fixed trait to its author. Name the relevant section, sentence, or omission. Explain the effect on a reader so that revision has a purpose. Specific praise is useful too because it shows what should be retained.
examples: The opening defines the problem clearly.
The second paragraph introduces a new term without explaining it.

content.heading: Make the next step achievable
content.text: Separate essential corrections from optional suggestions. A request such as add the missing comparison is clearer than make it better. Calibrate your tone to the relationship and consequences, while avoiding vague hedges that hide a required action. Explain uncertainty when you are unsure of the intended meaning.
examples: Please add the comparison required by the brief.
If you mean annual income, label the axis accordingly.

content.heading: Practise a three-part comment
content.text: Choose a paragraph from your own writing. Write feedback that identifies one feature, explains its impact, and suggests a revision. Limit the comment to the most useful change rather than listing every possible improvement. Apply the revision yourself and check whether the reader now has the missing information.
examples: The pronoun this has two possible referents; replace it with the specific policy name.
The conclusion introduces a new claim; develop it earlier or remove it.

questions.prompt: Which feedback is most actionable?
options: You are bad at clarity.
Improve absolutely everything.
This is confusing somehow.
Paragraph two uses this ambiguously; name the policy it refers to.
questions.explanation: The comment locates a specific issue and gives a concrete revision.

questions.prompt: Why distinguish required changes from optional suggestions?
options: So the writer can prioritize and understand what must be corrected.
So the writer can ignore the brief.
So the feedback can avoid all detail.
So every personal preference becomes a rule.
questions.explanation: Priority helps the writer direct effort toward the task requirements.

questions.prompt: Which comment explains the reader impact?
options: Use better English.
Define the term before using it so new readers can follow the comparison.
This paragraph exists.
Write something sophisticated.
questions.explanation: The comment connects a specific revision with the reader’s ability to understand the comparison.

lessons.title: Plan a purposeful formal letter
lessons.description: Practise an unofficial IELTS General Training style response.

content.heading: Identify relationship and purpose
content.text: This unofficial practice lesson uses a letter about a disrupted course. Before drafting, identify the recipient, your relationship, and the outcome you want. A letter to an administrator needs enough context to locate the issue, but a long personal history can bury the request. Choose a greeting appropriate to the known name and local convention.
examples: Purpose: explain cancelled sessions and request a replacement arrangement.
Recipient: the administrator responsible for the evening course.

content.heading: Give every requested point a role
content.text: Practice prompt: Write to a course administrator. Explain which sessions were cancelled, describe how this affected your study, and suggest a solution. Plan one clear function for each part. Use accurate dates and neutral descriptions, then make a practical request instead of relying on anger to communicate urgency.
examples: Two evening sessions were cancelled without replacement.
Could you offer an alternative session or access to a tutor?

content.heading: Review for task coverage and tone
content.text: Draft the letter, then label the sentence that addresses each requested point. Check whether the administrator can identify the course and act on your request. Remove exaggerated accusations and unsupported motives. End with a clear expectation for a reply, choosing a reasonable date if the situation requires one.
examples: Please let me know what arrangements are available before the next unit begins.
Please confirm whether a tutor session can replace the cancelled lessons.

questions.prompt: Which plan covers the practice prompt fully?
options: Greeting, childhood story, goodbye
Only a refund demand without context
Cancelled sessions, study impact, proposed solution
A list of unrelated courses
questions.explanation: The plan directly addresses all three requested points.

questions.prompt: Which sentence best states an actionable request?
options: The situation is unbelievable.
Everything about the course is terrible.
I have many feelings about studying.
Could you arrange a replacement session before the next unit?
questions.explanation: The recipient can understand the specific action and relevant time frame.

questions.prompt: What is the best final review question?
options: Can the recipient identify the issue and understand the requested response?
Have I used as many rare words as possible?
Have I accused the recipient of hidden motives?
Have I removed all course details?
questions.explanation: A purposeful letter supplies enough information for the recipient to act.

lessons.title: Join an academic discussion
lessons.description: Build on another contribution and ask a focused question.

content.heading: Connect before extending
content.text: An effective seminar contribution shows its relationship to the discussion. Briefly identify the previous point, then add a reason, example, or qualification. Repeating another person’s whole argument wastes time; introducing an unrelated speech breaks the thread. Name the idea accurately before agreeing with or challenging it.
examples: Building on your point about access, transport costs may matter too.
Your example concerns universities; would the same reasoning apply to schools?

content.heading: Clarify without pretending agreement
content.text: A question can test the meaning or evidence behind a claim. Ask what a key term includes or how a conclusion follows from a finding. Use a neutral tone and give the speaker space to answer. A clarification question is especially useful when disagreement may depend on different definitions.
examples: When you say participation, do you mean attendance or speaking in class?
What evidence links the change in attendance to the new timetable?

content.heading: Record a connected contribution
content.text: Imagine a classmate says online classes improve participation. Record a short reply that acknowledges the possibility, defines one relevant outcome, and asks a specific follow-up question. Listen for a clear link to the original claim. Replace filler phrases with a brief pause when you need time to choose a word.
examples: Attendance might rise, but do we know whether more students contribute to discussion?
Perhaps access improved, although the quality of interaction needs separate evidence.

questions.prompt: Which contribution clearly builds on an existing idea?
options: I prepared an unrelated speech yesterday.
Your point about access also raises a question about transport costs.
There is nothing to discuss.
Let us ignore everything already said.
questions.explanation: It names the previous idea and extends it with a relevant factor.

questions.prompt: Which question clarifies the meaning of participation?
options: Why are you always wrong?
Can I read my whole essay?
Do you mean attending sessions or contributing during them?
Is education a word?
questions.explanation: The question distinguishes two plausible meanings that could affect the argument.

questions.prompt: What should a useful follow-up question target?
options: The speaker’s personality
Any unrelated topic
Only vocabulary that sounds impressive
A particular definition, reason, or evidence gap
questions.explanation: Focused follow-up questions advance the discussion by addressing the substance of the contribution.

lessons.title: Use sentence stress to show contrast
lessons.description: Make the important correction audible without speeding up.

content.heading: Stress changes the intended contrast
content.text: English speakers often emphasize a word to signal what is new, corrected, or contrasted. In “I wanted the BLUE folder,” the focus distinguishes colour; in “I WANTED the blue folder,” it can contrast wanting with receiving. Capitals here mark practice emphasis, not a requirement to shout or use one fixed pitch.
examples: I requested THREE copies, not two.
Maya reviewed the draft; she did not WRITE it.

content.heading: Group ideas into thought units
content.text: Pause where an idea can be understood, especially before a contrast or after a long introductory phrase. Keep important grammatical connections together. A slower, well-grouped explanation can sound clearer than a fast uninterrupted sentence. Intonation varies across speakers and settings, so aim for intelligible meaning rather than imitation of one accent.
examples: If the figures are accurate / we can proceed / but we still need approval.
The first option is cheaper / whereas the second includes support.

content.heading: Practise two interpretations
content.text: Record the sentence “We need the final version today” twice. First emphasize final to contrast it with a draft; then emphasize today to contrast it with tomorrow. Add a short explanation after each recording and check whether the audible focus matches that explanation. Ask a listener to identify the intended correction if possible.
examples: We need the FINAL version today, rather than another draft.
We need the final version TODAY, rather than tomorrow.

questions.prompt: In “I requested THREE copies, not two,” what does the emphasis correct?
options: The quantity
The identity of the requester
The delivery address
The colour of the paper
questions.explanation: Three contrasts directly with two, making quantity the focus.

questions.prompt: Which grouping best preserves a conditional idea?
options: If the / figures are / accurate we can / proceed.
If the figures are accurate / we can proceed.
If / the figures are accurate we / can proceed.
If the figures / are accurate we can / proceed.
questions.explanation: The pause follows the complete condition and separates it from the main consequence.

questions.prompt: You mean a final version rather than a draft. Which word is the best focus?
options: We
Need in every possible context
Final
Today
questions.explanation: Final carries the specific contrast between the completed version and a draft.

lessons.title: Answer an interview with evidence
lessons.description: Use a concrete event, your action, and a bounded result.

content.heading: Choose an event with a clear role
content.text: For a question about solving a problem, choose one situation you can explain accurately. Give enough context to show the challenge, then distinguish your own action from the team’s work. A specific example is more credible than a list of flattering adjectives that any candidate could use.
examples: Our team missed updates because requests arrived through three channels.
I was responsible for tracking requests and noticed repeated omissions.

content.heading: Explain the result honestly
content.text: Describe what changed and how you know. Use a number only if it is accurate and you can explain its basis. If several factors contributed, avoid claiming sole credit. Mention a useful lesson or remaining limit when it helps show judgement rather than weakening every statement with unnecessary uncertainty.
examples: I introduced a shared request log; the team then tracked outstanding work more consistently.
Several changes helped, so I would not attribute the improvement to the log alone.

content.heading: Practise and adapt the answer
content.text: Record a concise response to “Tell me about a time you improved a process.” Include context, your action, an observed result, and reflection. Replay it to remove unrelated history. Practise a follow-up about what you would change next time, keeping your account consistent rather than memorizing a rigid script.
examples: Next time, I would involve support staff earlier when choosing the categories.
I would also check whether the system still works during busy periods.

questions.prompt: Which detail best demonstrates personal contribution?
options: We were all amazing.
The company has many employees.
Everyone knows I am organized.
I designed a shared log and tested it with two colleagues.
questions.explanation: The detail identifies an observable action performed by the candidate.

questions.prompt: When is a numerical result appropriate?
options: When it is accurate and its basis can be explained
Whenever a large number sounds impressive
Only when it guarantees future success
When it conceals other contributors
questions.explanation: Evidence should support the claim; an invented or unexplained number undermines credibility.

questions.prompt: Which reflection shows practical learning?
options: I would never change anything regardless of evidence.
Next time I would involve support staff before finalizing the categories.
The only lesson is that I am perfect.
I would use a larger invented percentage.
questions.explanation: The reflection identifies a concrete improvement linked to the process described.

lessons.title: Distinguish formal demands from facts
lessons.description: Use mandative clauses and remote forms with exact intent.

content.heading: A recommendation is not a report
content.text: After verbs such as recommend, insist, and require, a that-clause can express a desired action. In a formal mandative construction, the base form remains unchanged even with a singular subject. A should construction is also possible in many varieties. Compare this with a statement describing what actually happens.
examples: The panel recommends that she be appointed.
The panel reports that she is appointed each year.

content.heading: Read the meaning of insist
content.text: Insist can express a demand or a firm assertion, so the surrounding grammar and context matter. “He insists that she leave” presents a requested action; “He insists that she left” reports his firm claim about a past event. Do not treat every clause after insist as a demand.
examples: They insisted that the file be removed.
They insisted that the file had already disappeared.

content.heading: Practise intention and evidence
content.text: Write one sentence proposing that a named person take responsibility, then a second reporting that the person already has responsibility. Explain the difference aloud. Finally revise a demand into a polite request for a colleague, keeping the desired action clear while adapting its interpersonal force.
examples: The committee recommends that Arun lead the review.
Could Arun lead the review, subject to his availability?

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses a formal mandative base form?
options: The board requires that each applicant is being yesterday.
The board requires each applicant be to notified.
The board requires that each applicant be notified.
The board requires that each applicant being notified.
questions.explanation: Be is the unchanged base form in the that-clause expressing a requirement.

questions.prompt: “He insists that she left yesterday” most naturally reports what?
options: A demand that she leave tomorrow
An instruction to change the calendar
A question about her plans
A firm assertion about a past event
questions.explanation: Left yesterday presents an asserted past event rather than a desired future action.

questions.prompt: Which pair distinguishes a recommendation from an established fact?
options: They recommend that she lead; they confirm that she leads.
She leads; she leads.
They recommend she leading; they confirm she leaded.
They lead her; they lead her again.
questions.explanation: The base-form mandative expresses desired action; the indicative leads reports the stated situation.

lessons.title: Use ellipsis without losing the meaning
lessons.description: Avoid repetition while keeping missing material recoverable.

content.heading: Let context supply the missing words
content.text: Ellipsis omits language that a reader can recover from the context. “Mira can attend, and Jo can too” avoids repeating attend. In comparative and coordinated structures, omission can create elegant economy, but it also creates ambiguity if two different antecedents are equally plausible. Brevity is valuable only when interpretation stays stable.
examples: Mira has finished, but Jo has not.
Some chose the train; others, the bus.

content.heading: Choose a suitable substitute
content.text: So can substitute for a proposition after verbs such as think and hope: “Will it work? I think so.” Do so can replace a previously mentioned action, especially in formal writing. Make sure the substitute refers to the intended claim or action, rather than to a nearby noun or a different event.
examples: Jo promised to check the attachment; she will do so today.
Will they agree? I hope so.

content.heading: Restore before compressing
content.text: Take a paragraph with repeated verbs and identify two places where omission would help. Rewrite the full versions first so the intended meaning is explicit. Then compress them and ask whether another interpretation has appeared. Restore the noun or verb when economy creates uncertainty about who did what.
examples: Rina reviewed the draft, and Omar reviewed it too.
Rina reviewed the draft, and Omar did too.

questions.prompt: In “Mira has finished, but Jo has not,” what is omitted after not?
options: Mira
Finished
Has
But
questions.explanation: The prior clause supplies the repeated past participle finished.

questions.prompt: What does so represent in “Will they agree? I hope so”?
options: Only the noun they
An instruction to leave
The proposition that they will agree
The opposite of agreement
questions.explanation: So substitutes for the positive proposition in the preceding question.

questions.prompt: When should repeated wording be restored?
options: Whenever a sentence contains two people
Whenever a paragraph is formal
Only when a reader requests more adjectives
When its omission leaves the intended reference ambiguous
questions.explanation: Recoverability is the condition that makes ellipsis clear and useful.

lessons.title: Place information where readers need it
lessons.description: Use clefts and end focus without changing the underlying claim.

content.heading: Separate the message from its packaging
content.text: Different grammatical structures can foreground different parts of the same event. A cleft such as “It was Priya who corrected the file” focuses attention on the person. A pseudo-cleft such as “What we need is a reliable backup” foregrounds the required item. Use these structures when the contrast matters, not as decoration.
examples: It was Priya who corrected the file, not Alex.
What the team needs is a reliable backup.

content.heading: Build from known information
content.text: Readers often follow a sentence more easily when it begins with an established topic and moves toward important new information. This is a tendency rather than an absolute rule. In a paragraph about a report, “The report was reviewed by two independent specialists” can connect more smoothly than suddenly beginning with the specialists.
examples: We commissioned a report. The report was reviewed independently.
The independent review identified a missing comparison.

content.heading: Revise for a deliberate focus
content.text: Write a neutral sentence about a successful change. Rewrite it to highlight the person responsible, then the action that mattered. Check that your versions do not accidentally imply an exclusive claim unsupported by the evidence. Read the paragraph around each version to judge which transition serves the reader best.
examples: Nila improved the process by simplifying the form.
What Nila changed was the form itself.

questions.prompt: What does “It was Priya who corrected the file” foreground?
options: The identity of the person who corrected it
The file’s colour
The date of a future review
The number of corrections
questions.explanation: The cleft focuses attention on Priya, often contrasting her with another possible person.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses a pseudo-cleft?
options: We need a reliable backup.
What we need is a reliable backup.
A backup is reliable.
We will back up the file.
questions.explanation: The what-clause identifies a variable and the following clause supplies the focused answer.

questions.prompt: Why might a passive suit a paragraph already discussing a report?
options: It automatically makes any claim true.
It always removes all responsibility.
It can keep the report as the established topic.
It prevents mention of the reviewer.
questions.explanation: Information packaging can preserve a topic while placing the reviewer or finding later in the sentence.

lessons.title: Choose the exact strength of a claim
lessons.description: Distinguish plausible, compelling, conclusive, and inevitable.

content.heading: Separate possibility from justification
content.text: Plausible describes an account that appears reasonable; compelling suggests strong persuasive force; conclusive describes evidence sufficient to settle a question in context. These words are not interchangeable upgrades. The appropriate strength depends on the quality of support and the alternatives that remain open, rather than the writer’s enthusiasm.
examples: The explanation is plausible, but competing accounts remain.
The test supplied compelling evidence, although replication is needed.

content.heading: Distinguish tendency from necessity
content.text: Likely concerns probability; inevitable implies an outcome cannot be avoided; prevalent describes how widespread something is. A widespread practice is not necessarily desirable or unavoidable. Words controlling scope matter too: some, many, and all make substantially different commitments even when the rest of the sentence is identical.
examples: The practice is prevalent in this sample.
A delay is likely, but not inevitable.

content.heading: Revise an inflated paragraph
content.text: Write a short claim about a training programme using likely, then list what evidence would justify that judgement. Replace any accidental universal statement with a bounded one. Compare plausible and conclusive in your revision and explain why the available observation supports one strength rather than the other.
examples: The pilot makes a benefit plausible; it does not establish that all teams will improve.
Most respondents reported progress, rather than all employees.

questions.prompt: Which word suggests an explanation is reasonable without settling the issue?
options: Conclusive
Inevitable
Unavoidable
Plausible
questions.explanation: Plausible indicates credible possibility, leaving room for alternative explanations.

questions.prompt: What does prevalent describe?
options: How widespread something is
Whether it is morally right
Whether it cannot be avoided
Whether it has been causally proved
questions.explanation: Prevalent concerns frequency or spread, not desirability or necessity.

questions.prompt: Which statement makes the weakest commitment?
options: Every participant will benefit.
Some participants may benefit.
Benefit is inevitable for all.
No participant can fail to benefit.
questions.explanation: Some and may restrict both the group and the certainty of the claim.

lessons.title: Interpret understatement with care
lessons.description: Read softened criticism without inventing a hidden message.

content.heading: Recognize a possible interpersonal function
content.text: Understatement deliberately expresses less intensity than a situation might suggest. “The timetable is a little ambitious” may soften a concern that the schedule is unrealistic. Interpretation depends on context, relationship, and delivery. Do not assume a polite phrase always has one secret meaning or that a cultural stereotype predicts every speaker.
examples: That may be difficult by Friday.
I have a few reservations about the proposed sequence.

content.heading: Check an inference against evidence
content.text: A softened objection becomes clearer when it is followed by a reason, condition, or alternative. “We still need approval” is a concrete constraint. If the implication matters, ask a neutral clarification question instead of acting on a guess. Distinguish recognizing indirectness from attributing hostility that the speaker has not expressed.
examples: Do you mean Friday is unlikely, or that you need another resource?
Would Monday be a more workable date?

content.heading: Practise both sides of a repair
content.text: Role-play a colleague expressing concern indirectly, then a listener checking the intended action. Make the final agreement explicit so politeness does not leave responsibility unclear. Repeat with a direct but respectful version and compare which wording suits an urgent operational decision.
examples: Indirect concern: The scope is rather broad for one week.
Confirmed action: We will reduce the first release to two features.

questions.prompt: “The timetable is a little ambitious” may function as what?
options: A guaranteed promise to meet it
A declaration that no work is required
A softened concern about feasibility
Proof of personal hostility
questions.explanation: In the right context, the phrase raises a feasibility concern indirectly; context is still needed.

questions.prompt: What is the best response when the practical implication is unclear?
options: Assume the colleague secretly hates the project.
Treat the phrase as unconditional agreement.
Ignore the concern because it is polite.
Ask whether the date is unlikely and what change would help.
questions.explanation: A clarification question checks the inference and moves toward an actionable understanding.

questions.prompt: Why make the final agreement explicit?
options: Polite indirectness can otherwise leave action and responsibility unclear.
Indirect speech has no meaning.
Every speaker uses the same code.
Explicit actions prevent all future changes.
questions.explanation: An explicit agreement establishes what people will do while preserving respectful tone.

lessons.title: Notice how metaphors frame an issue
lessons.description: Compare useful images with their hidden assumptions.

content.heading: A metaphor highlights selected features
content.text: Calling a policy a safety net emphasizes protection against a fall; calling it a springboard emphasizes movement toward opportunity. Both images can be useful, but neither describes every feature of the policy. Ask what the image draws attention to and what it makes easier to overlook.
examples: A safety net highlights protection.
A springboard highlights a route toward further action.

content.heading: Avoid treating an image as proof
content.text: A metaphor organizes thought; it is not evidence that the comparison holds in every respect. Language describing a debate as a battle may imply winners and losers where cooperation is possible. In analytical writing, explain the literal claim and assess that claim using relevant information.
examples: The initiative is a bridge between training and employment.
Literal question: Does it help participants move into suitable work?

content.heading: Reframe and test the consequence
content.text: Choose an education policy and describe it with two different images. Write the practical assumptions each image invites. Then produce a neutral explanation that names the actual mechanism and intended outcome. Compare which details disappear when your description relies entirely on the image.
examples: A ladder suggests upward stages; a network suggests several possible routes.
The programme offers different entry points rather than one compulsory sequence.

questions.prompt: What aspect does the metaphor safety net foreground?
options: Guaranteed upward promotion
Protection against a harmful fall or setback
The exact cost of a policy
Proof that every participant benefits equally
questions.explanation: The image emphasizes support when someone faces a setback.

questions.prompt: Why is a metaphor insufficient as evidence?
options: Metaphors cannot communicate ideas.
All figurative language is ungrammatical.
An image selects a comparison but does not establish its factual accuracy.
An image automatically includes every mechanism.
questions.explanation: The literal claim still needs relevant evidence beyond the persuasive comparison.

questions.prompt: Which literal question tests “a bridge between training and employment”?
options: What colour is the imaginary bridge?
Are all classrooms made from concrete?
How can every other policy be ignored?
Does the initiative help participants move into suitable work?
questions.explanation: The question translates the image into the intended mechanism and outcome.

lessons.title: Detect a misleading comparison
lessons.description: Check units, group composition, and the level of a conclusion.

content.heading: Original passage: the efficiency league table
content.text: A magazine ranked community clinics by the average time spent with each visitor. The clinic with the shortest appointments was labelled the most efficient. Its director welcomed the attention but questioned the comparison. Her clinic handled many routine vaccinations, while another served people with several long-term conditions. A short appointment could reflect a straightforward task rather than better organization. Conversely, a longer consultation might prevent repeated visits, a benefit the table did not measure. The magazine replied that readers wanted a simple guide and that appointment length was at least easy to compare. Simplicity, the director argued, did not solve the mismatch between the measure and the judgement. She proposed reporting several indicators, including follow-up needs and patient understanding, with explanations of the services each clinic provided. The issue was not whether time mattered, but whether one average could fairly rank unlike activities.
examples: Measured indicator: average appointment duration.
Unmeasured possibilities: task complexity and prevented repeat visits.

content.heading: Inspect the comparison before the ranking
content.text: A common unit does not guarantee comparable underlying tasks. Identify what the metric measures directly and what the label most efficient adds. The passage supplies reasons why appointment length may vary, but it does not prove that any particular clinic is better or worse overall.
examples: Shorter average time can reflect simpler appointments.
A routine vaccination and a complex consultation may require different time.

content.heading: Write a bounded evaluation
content.text: State the strongest conclusion the table supports and one conclusion it cannot support by itself. Then propose an additional indicator and explain why it matters. Avoid reversing the magazine’s mistake by assuming that longer appointments always demonstrate better care.
examples: The table compares duration; a fair efficiency judgement requires further context.
Lower follow-up demand could be relevant to an overall efficiency judgement.

questions.prompt: What is the director’s main objection?
options: The ranking treats unlike activities as though one time average captured efficiency.
The ranking does not account for the absolute number of staff at each clinic.
The magazine should rank clinics only by patient satisfaction instead.
Long consultations are necessarily more efficient than short ones.
questions.explanation: The director challenges the match between the measure and an overall efficiency ranking across different services.

questions.prompt: Which possible benefit of longer consultations is absent from the table?
options: Reducing the complexity of the patients’ existing conditions
Avoiding repeated visits
Improving the accuracy of the magazine’s attendance count
Guaranteeing that every patient understands the consultation
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly notes that a longer consultation might prevent repeated visits.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion would repeat the same oversimplification in reverse?
options: The services included in each average differ.
Time is relevant but cannot capture every consequence.
The clinic with the longest appointments must be the best.
Additional indicators could improve the comparison.
questions.explanation: Assuming longest is best still turns one incomplete measure into an overall judgement.

lessons.title: Follow a counterargument precisely
lessons.description: Distinguish rejecting a principle from limiting its application.

content.heading: Original passage: open meetings
content.text: Publishing every committee discussion sounds like an uncomplicated victory for accountability. Citizens should certainly be able to inspect decisions that affect them, and secrecy can protect poor judgement. Yet a public record of every preliminary remark may encourage participants to arrive with rehearsed positions and avoid exploring uncertain alternatives. That possibility does not justify private decision-making as a general rule. It suggests a distinction between the evidence and reasons that must accompany a final decision and the provisional conversation through which those reasons develop. Any limited private session would need a stated purpose, an expiry point, and a subsequent explanation of what was decided. Otherwise, the exception could swallow the principle. The choice is therefore not between total exposure and unreviewable secrecy. It is between arrangements that make power answerable while allowing thought to develop, and arrangements that fail one of those responsibilities.
examples: The writer endorses accountability.
The proposed exception includes purpose, expiry, and later explanation.

content.heading: Track the boundary words
content.text: Certainly concedes an important principle, while yet introduces a complication. The warning that an exception could swallow the principle limits the writer’s own proposal. Follow the full sequence before assigning a position. A counterargument can refine a principle’s implementation rather than reject the principle itself.
examples: Private exploration is not presented as permission for unreviewable decisions.
A stated expiry point prevents an exception from becoming indefinite.

content.heading: Test a faithful paraphrase
content.text: Write a summary that includes both accountability and the danger of rehearsed discussion. Name two safeguards attached to any private session. Then test your summary against an extreme alternative: would a reader mistakenly think the writer supports permanent secrecy or publication of every tentative comment?
examples: The writer proposes limited space for exploration under explicit accountability safeguards.
The passage rejects both unreviewable secrecy and an unqualified exposure rule.

questions.prompt: What principle does the writer retain?
options: Every preliminary remark should remain private indefinitely.
Preliminary conversations and final decisions require identical publication rules.
The public should inspect final choices only when committees volunteer reasons.
Public power must remain accountable.
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly supports inspection of decisions and requires explanations and safeguards.

questions.prompt: What concern motivates a limited exception?
options: Total exposure may discourage uncertain exploration and encourage rehearsed positions.
Public records are inherently less accurate than private recollections.
Publication prevents citizens from understanding the final decision.
Uncertain ideas cannot be explained in a later public account.
questions.explanation: The concern is about how unrestricted publication might shape preliminary discussion.

questions.prompt: What does “the exception could swallow the principle” warn against?
options: Any private exploration is automatically equivalent to permanent secrecy.
A limited permission expanding until it undermines accountability
A later explanation can replace the need for any stated limit.
An expiry point would make preliminary discussion impossible.
questions.explanation: The metaphor warns that an exception without controls could defeat the broader rule it qualifies.

lessons.title: Read rhetoric and evidence together
lessons.description: Separate an attractive conclusion from the support it receives.

content.heading: Original passage: the smart city slogan
content.text: The city’s campaign calls its sensor network “a listening city.” The phrase is appealing: traffic signals adapt, water leaks are flagged, and waste collections follow measured demand. Such systems can improve services, but listening usually implies more than detecting a signal. Residents may tell officials that a quiet street needs a crossing even when few recorded journeys reveal the need. A parent who avoids the route because it feels unsafe leaves little traffic data behind. The campaign’s metaphor risks treating measured activity as the whole public voice. This does not make the sensors useless, nor does a personal account automatically outweigh every measurement. It means that officials must examine what each kind of evidence can reveal and what it can miss. A city listens more fully when it creates ways for unrecorded needs to enter a decision, rather than merely giving its devices a sympathetic name.
examples: Sensor data describe detected activity.
Avoided routes can conceal unmet needs.

content.heading: Identify the rhetorical target
content.text: The writer questions the completeness suggested by a slogan while accepting potential practical benefits. Distinguish criticism of a framing device from rejection of the technology. The parent example introduces missing activity: absence from the data may reflect avoidance rather than lack of need.
examples: The criticism concerns equating measurement with the entire public voice.
The writer accepts service benefits while challenging the slogan’s completeness.

content.heading: Synthesize the evidence principle
content.text: Write a two-sentence conclusion explaining why both measurements and accounts matter. Preserve the statement that neither form automatically outranks the other. For advanced reading practice, identify the sentence that prevents a simplistic pro-technology or anti-technology interpretation.
examples: Different evidence can reveal different aspects of a public need.
A personal account can reveal avoidance that low traffic counts leave unexplained.

questions.prompt: What does the avoided-route example demonstrate?
